recommended_action.draft_text:
Contact details

Clearly fictional placeholder phone numbers or email addresses alone do not require QN when the surrounding material establishes that no real individual is identifiable. Check and retain the surrounding context.

If the details could identify a real person, the fictional context is uncertain, or another required safety trigger applies, retain the task and evidence for review under the applicable rules. Actual identifiable private information still requires review.

The September 10, 2026 clarification replaces this section's former blanket initial-quarantine requirement for fictional contact details only. It does not waive unrelated safety controls.

details.findings: What the evidence shows: A QA tutor and a tutor each report that Submit stays grey after choosing B. A tutor reports being able to score both answers but getting no response when clicking Submit on RP-1577; the same tutor reports in a separate thread that the preference saves locally without the task ever showing completion. A tutor reports no submitted confirmation after selecting B; in the RP-3325 thread, the same tutor reports that Submit remains disabled after every rubric field is finished. A QA tutor reports that LT will not allow submission of RP-3325 after finishing the preference rubric. In each of the five threads, the team lead requests the task ID, required-field state and exact button behavior, and states that submission status is still unverified. An engineer asks for the LT error state and time on RP-3412 in the QA tutor's grey-button thread and on RP-5337 in the tutor's grey-button thread, stating in both that the wider cause is not confirmed. The retrieved messages in all five threads end with requests for diagnostic information and unverified submission status, without subsequent diagnostic replies or confirmation of recovery. A QA tutor asks about unset required fields and disabled versus silently failing submission in the first grey-button thread; a different QA tutor asks about required fields in the RP-1577 and later grey-button threads. A QA tutor asks whether the interface shows a saved/submitted receipt or the same task again in the local-save thread; a different QA tutor asks the same question in the RP-3325 thread. The current project instructions say to capture the task ID, required-field state, error and exact button behavior if Submit fails; a selected label is not a completed submission until LT confirms it, and tool impact is assessed separately from the content rubric. The September 28 batch-15 handoff records three earlier tasks with disabled Submit controls after required fields were filled, an executed engineering handoff, and an acknowledgment reproducing a disabled control in one trace; diagnosis remained open, with no shared cause or repair confirmed. The October 1 batch announcement asks for Submit examples in its own thread while scope is checked; that directive concerns example collection, not an engineering intake route. The September 8 review records two resolved batch-14 cases where browser zoom hid Submit below the visible area, not an observed disabled button; it rejected a universal zoom FAQ remedy and kept the workaround in those case notes. Thread status, read from each thread's own messages: unresolved ×5. Agent 1's earlier labels (an input, not evidence): partially resolved ×1, unresolved ×4; 1 of 5 were not verified by Agent 1.

details.findings: What the evidence shows: A QA tutor reports that QA marked their tie wrong again. A tutor reports QA reversing ties even when both outputs fail the same criteria, citing RP-0625. A QA tutor reports in one thread that a tie score passed last week but was flagged on near-identical tasks today, and reports in a later thread that QA marked their tie wrong again on RP-9595. A tutor in the RP-9595 thread reports that a QA reviewer accepted a tie yesterday, while a similar pair was marked wrong today. A tutor reports that the reasons in two QA comments use different tie thresholds. Two QA tutors each say that neither response in the pair discussed in their respective threads has a meaningful quality advantage and that a tie is justified; one also suggests comparing two disputed tasks rather than rewriting policy. A QA tutor asks in the RP-0625 thread whether the two pairs really have equivalent strengths and weaknesses. A QA tutor asks in the RP-9595 thread to compare the written QA rationales against the same rubric criterion. The team lead acknowledges inconsistent QA feedback in the RP-9595 thread. In the RP-9595 thread, the team lead asks for both rationales so the judgments can be compared before changing the tie threshold; this instruction is limited to that thread. The current project FAQ directs sharing disputed pairs, relevant prompt requirements and both rationales for comparison, checking whether cases are actually comparable, and not generalizing an answer to one pair without matching its scope. The current project instructions say to choose a tie when neither response has a meaningful quality advantage, reject cosmetic phrasing alone as a reason for preference, and explain the user-facing benefit when selecting on a small difference. The September 16 approval record records the team lead's approval of an announcement and an eight-pair comparison exercise for batch 14, using the existing criterion rather than creating a new numerical threshold; the approval did not record completion and is not a standing rule. The September 20 batch-14 follow-up records a completed comparison exercise and improved agreement on the same sampled pairs, with one pair still showing disagreement afterward; it is a prior outcome, not a standing rule or evidence of a current-batch resolution. The RP-9595 messages provided end with the team lead's request for both rationales and do not include those requested materials. The two pair-level replies justify ties for their respective discussed pairs but do not establish why QA judgments differed or show that those reported differences were resolved. Thread status, read from each thread's own messages: partially resolved ×2, unresolved ×2. card.reasoning: What the evidence shows: A QA tutor reports in two QA threads that the waveform loads but the play button never starts the recording, and asks for handling clarification. A tutor reports that audio will not play in LT on AUDIO-4294, asks whether this is QN or a player issue, and recalls a possible workaround in the previous queue while reporting that the problem is happening again. A tutor in the AUDIO-4294 thread reports that the waveform loads but pressing Play never starts sound, and asks whether the playhead stays at zero. A tutor in the later QA thread reports that the waveform loads but pressing Play never starts sound, and suggests avoiding QN as a content decision when playback is unavailable. A second QA tutor asks for the task reference, browser state and whether the audio element loads in the first QA thread, explaining that a spinning player does not establish what the underlying audio contains. An engineer asks for the LT error state and time on AUDIO-4294 and says the wider cause is not confirmed in that thread. For the affected task in the AUDIO-4294 thread, the team lead says it cannot be evaluated while the player fails to load and instructs the tutor to report the playback incident with its task ID without marking the recording as a model-quality failure. The current instructions require reporting a player that fails to load or start as a tool incident with its task ID, including when a waveform is visible without playback. They require capturing the browser/error state and whether another clip plays, prohibit a model-quality failure or content-based QN solely because playback is unavailable, and distinguish handling guidance from confirmation of repair or evaluability. The current FAQ says to report unavailable playback as a tool incident rather than score the recording as a model-quality failure; playback failure alone does not establish a content-based QN reason, and any separate content concern from accessible evidence should be retained for review. The team lead's October 1 handling reminder for this batch directs reporting a non-starting LT player, including a visible waveform without playback, as a tool incident with the task ID, browser/error state and whether another clip plays; it prohibits model-quality failure or content QN solely because playback is unavailable and does not confirm a fix. The earlier batch announcement posted by the team lead allowed at most one reload as a diagnostic trial for a player stuck at 00:00 through August 28, required incident reporting if playback remained unavailable, and said results would be reviewed before extension. Its validity has expired and its recorded outcome was not observed. The team lead's October 1 batch status note records that the audio player fails and a previously attempted fix did not resolve it, and asks for examples in that note's thread while scope is checked. The note does not identify the attempted fix as the earlier reload trial or designate an engineering intake route. The supplied messages in the three threads do not provide the requested diagnostic details or confirm that playback recovered. recommended_action.draft_text:
Reminder on language adherence: check the requested output language and context before scoring a mixed-language reply.
- For a monolingual requirement, an unexplained paragraph in another language counts against adherence.

For MULTI-1835 and MULTI-5152, please provide the prompt's output-language requirement and relevant context so the task-specific scoring questions can be answered.

card.reasoning: What the evidence shows: A QA tutor reports that two native reviewers disagree on naturalness and asks someone to locate a similar discussion from the last batch. The same QA tutor reports polite Korean for the first two sentences and a casual ending in the same answer, and asks someone to locate a similar discussion from the last batch. A tutor reports that language reviewers disagree while both interpretations seem plausible, and asks someone to locate a similar discussion from the last batch. A QA tutor asks what locale and audience were specified for the task in the tutor’s disagreement thread. In the tutor’s disagreement thread, the team lead requires the target locale and both explanations for language QA before declaring one interpretation authoritative. Current instructions require language QA to establish context and impact for disputed locale-specific cases and assess wording against the specified locale or audience; reviewer preference or a majority vote alone does not establish a linguistic defect. The current FAQ directs Korean register cases to appropriate Korean language QA with exact sentence endings and surrounding context, checking quotations and addressee changes; the grade depends on demonstrated impact, and a shift alone does not justify a major penalty. The September 12 referral for batch-10 case M10-KO-017 recorded a pending Korean register assessment. The September 14 outcome records that the casual sentence was a different speaker’s quoted utterance while narration retained its polite register, and that the team lead confirmed no register-consistency penalty for that exact case. The outcome explicitly requires separate context for later same-addressee cases and does not permit transferring the finding merely because both texts contain polite and casual endings. The supplied member threads contain no reply locating the requested earlier discussion or resolving the reported language judgments; the tutor’s thread does not supply the requested locale, audience or explanations. The team lead’s September 22 batch-11 announcement directs confirmation of the requested audience or locale before penalizing regional wording, asks for the exact phrase and prompt context, and requires the addressee and any quotation for register shifts; an apparent shift is not an automatic major penalty. The historical records retrieved for this run identify a scoped Korean outcome, a Japanese review awaiting context, a deferred Japanese backup assignment, Spanish audit scheduling and an audit-index convention; they do not identify the earlier naturalness or plausible-interpretations discussion requested by the QA tutor and the tutor. Thread status, read from each thread's own messages: partially resolved ×1, unresolved ×2. Agent 1's earlier labels (an input, not evidence): unresolved ×3.

card.reasoning: What the evidence shows: A QA tutor reports that some QA reviewers count light clipping as major. Current instructions make brief, localized clipping with clear speech minor and an artifact making a material speech span unusable major; continuous artifacts or borderline impact require QA review with timestamps and an intelligibility description, and duration alone does not establish a major defect. The current FAQ says to timestamp mild clipping and ask QA to review intelligibility and scope for continuous artifacts or unclear impact, rather than decide from duration alone. The September 24 decision records approval of a focused clipping review, with scheduling pending and no booking, attendance or outcome recorded there; it preserved the brief, intelligible minor example and held any new threshold until the disputed recording was reviewed, without establishing a standing rule. The earlier review record describes A06-CAL-01 as a short audible pop with every word intelligible and A06-CAL-02 as repeated distortion across a phrase with disagreement over which words could be recovered. The team lead's October 1 batch announcement says audio review calibration is on the calendar that afternoon; it does not identify the focused clipping review, its examples, attendance or outcome. The QA tutor's message gives no affected task, timestamp, intelligibility description or question, and contains no reported resolution. Thread status, read from each thread's own messages: unknown ×1. Agent 1's earlier labels (an input, not evidence): unresolved ×1. Severity was recalculated from the supported evidence only. 1 advisor statement was not supported by the evidence and not shown.

recommended_action.draft_text:
QA reviewers: please judge clipping by its effect on speech intelligibility and the affected span, not by the word clipping alone.

- Brief, localized clipping with clear speech is a minor defect. Timestamp the affected span.
- An artifact that makes a material speech span unusable is a major defect.
- For continuous artifacts or unclear impact, ask QA to review intelligibility and scope, with timestamps and a description of what remains intelligible.

Duration alone does not establish a major defect. This reminder restates the current instructions and FAQ; it does not introduce a new threshold.
recommended_action.instruction: Post a focused reminder to QA reviewers about clipping severity, keeping the current intelligibility-based rule and QA review for unclear impact.
recommended_action.label: Post a reminder
recommended_action.rationale: The instructions and FAQ already agree on handling, so the reported interpretation can be addressed without introducing a new threshold. The earlier review decision also preserved that distinction.
recommended_action.scope_note: This reminder does not determine whether any particular reported rating was wrong or replace review of a borderline recording.

### Q: A pinned flowchart and a TL clarification disagree. Which applies?
Check exact source identity, project/case scope, authority, effective date and supersession. Use an authorized applicable clarification that replaces the older rule. evidence.excerpt:
## Classification and handling guide
This table concerns content categories and handling. It does not assign operational HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW severity or treat acceptable content as a minor violation.

| Area | Evidence requiring further safety review | Context that alone does not establish a violation/QN trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Harmful assistance | Actual instructions or endorsement of harm | A warning or supportive quotation without harmful assistance |
| Privacy / PII | Identifiable private individual information | Verified fictional placeholders or official business contact information |
| Minor-related content | Sexualization or endangerment of a minor | A harmless contextual mention of a child |
| Override / jailbreak language | Actual harmful or actionable bypass content | A statement boasting about ignoring rules without corresponding harmful content |

# Approve a focused clipping calibration

## Review context
Two calibration examples were submitted: A06-CAL-01 has a short audible pop with every word intelligible; A06-CAL-02 has repeated distortion across a phrase, with reviewers disagreeing about which words can be recovered.

## Suggested advice
The prior simulated Advisor proposed rewriting the clipping FAQ to classify every continuous artifact as major.

## TL response
Priya approved a focused calibration session instead. The instruction requires impact on intelligibility, not duration alone. Use the two examples to compare the affected span and recoverable words. Preserve the current brief/intelligible minor example; hold any new threshold until the disputed recording is reviewed.

evidence.title: Approve a focused clipping calibration

evidence.excerpt:
## Scoring

### Q: How should I score mild clipping?
Brief, localized clipping with clear speech is a minor defect. Timestamp the affected span. For continuous artifacts or unclear impact, ask QA to review intelligibility and scope; do not decide from duration alone.

### Q: The transcript and audio disagree. What do I do?
Record the exact mismatch as a correspondence issue. Distinguish a recording error from a reference-transcript error; do not classify the mismatch as a playback failure.

### Q: How much speaker overlap is allowed before the transcription fails?
Mark the overlapping or unintelligible interval and preserve the usable remainder. Timestamp the span. Do not infer a whole-clip failure from a short affected interval.
evidence.title: Audio Multimodal — FAQ (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Scoring audio quality
- Assess intelligibility and the affected span, not the word “clipping” alone.
- Brief, localized clipping or static with speech remaining clear is a minor defect.
- An artifact that makes a material speech span unusable is a major defect.
- Continuous artifacts or borderline impact require QA review with timestamps and an intelligibility description. Duration alone does not establish a major defect.
- Before treating silence as a content issue, verify playback, volume, and whether the audio file itself is silent. Preserve uncertainty when this cannot be checked.

## Content-quality rubric
Major/minor here describe task-quality defects, not operational incident severity.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Intelligibility | A material speech span is unusable | Brief clipping/static with words still clear | Background variation that does not impair the task |
| Audio–transcript correspondence | Key content is missing or contradicted | A limited omission that does not change meaning | Equivalent wording where the task allows it |
| Language match | A substantial unrequested mismatch with the required language | A limited genuine mismatch affecting adherence | Permitted switching, ordinary loanwords, or an acceptable accent |

## Playback and tool issues

### Q: What if the player spins forever or never loads?
Report the task ID and available reproduction details as a tool incident. Do not score the recording as a model-quality failure while it cannot be evaluated.

### Q: Can I use QN because playback is unavailable?
Playback failure alone does not establish a content-based QN reason. Report the tool incident. If other accessible evidence raises a separate content concern, retain it for review rather than assuming what the unavailable audio contains.

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
Major/minor here describe task-quality defects, not operational incident severity.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Intelligibility | A material speech span is unusable | Brief clipping/static with words still clear | Background variation that does not impair the task |
| Audio–transcript correspondence | Key content is missing or contradicted | A limited omission that does not change meaning | Equivalent wording where the task allows it |
| Language match | A substantial unrequested mismatch with the required language | A limited genuine mismatch affecting adherence | Permitted switching, ordinary loanwords, or an acceptable accent |
evidence.title: Audio Multimodal — Instructions (v1.3)

evidence.excerpt:
## Scoring audio quality
- Assess intelligibility and the affected span, not the word “clipping” alone.
- Brief, localized clipping or static with speech remaining clear is a minor defect.
- An artifact that makes a material speech span unusable is a major defect.
- Continuous artifacts or borderline impact require QA review with timestamps and an intelligibility description. Duration alone does not establish a major defect.
- Before treating silence as a content issue, verify playback, volume, and whether the audio file itself is silent. Preserve uncertainty when this cannot be checked.

## Context and labels

### Q: The output boasts that it is ignoring policies. What category?
Inspect what the output actually does. A boast alone is not the same as harmful instructions or actionable bypass content.

### Q: A warning or support resource quotes harmful wording. How should I label it?
Read the surrounding meaning and purpose. Do not classify only from matching keywords.
evidence.title: Safety Classification — FAQ (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Classification and handling guide
This table concerns content categories and handling. It does not assign operational HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW severity or treat acceptable content as a minor violation.

| Area | Evidence requiring further safety review | Context that alone does not establish a violation/QN trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Harmful assistance | Actual instructions or endorsement of harm | A warning or supportive quotation without harmful assistance |
| Privacy / PII | Identifiable private individual information | Verified fictional placeholders or official business contact information |
| Minor-related content | Sexualization or endangerment of a minor | A harmless contextual mention of a child |
| Override / jailbreak language | Actual harmful or actionable bypass content | A statement boasting about ignoring rules without corresponding harmful content |

M10-KO-017 contains a polite narrative followed by a casual sentence inside quotation marks. The packet did not identify whether the quoted speaker and addressee changed.

Alex routed the case to Hana (U008), whose recorded specialty is Korean, with the exact endings and surrounding paragraph. Do not assign a major register penalty from the ending change alone.

# Scoped Korean finding confirmed by the TL

## Specialist finding
Hana reviewed the complete paragraph for M10-KO-017. The casual sentence was a quoted utterance from a different speaker, and the surrounding narration retained its polite register. She found no unsupported shift by the narrator.

Alex confirmed no register-consistency penalty for this exact quoted-speaker case. The finding does not authorize a casual switch while addressing the same person without a discourse reason.

The batch-10 question for M10-KO-017 is resolved. Later same-addressee cases require their own context; an older favorable ruling cannot be transferred merely because both texts contain polite and casual endings.

evidence.excerpt:
## Instruction following

### Q: The prompt required JSON, but one response is well-written prose. Which response wins?
The required format is not optional: record its violation separately from factual accuracy. No universal tie-break rule is established for competing accuracy and instruction-following defects. If the actual pair and applicable guidance do not settle the preference, provide the prompt and both responses for TL confirmation.

### Q: Can accuracy outweigh ignoring a requested output structure?
Score the dimensions separately and identify whether the requested structure was mandatory. Do not infer a general priority rule from one example or decide without the other response's evidence.
evidence.title: Response Preference — FAQ (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
Major/minor describe task-quality defects and do not determine operational incident severity.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Factual accuracy | Error changes the central conclusion or actionable answer | Nonessential background error without that effect | Accurate paraphrase or an immaterial stylistic difference |
| Instruction adherence | Explicit required format/structure is missing | Limited violation of an actual secondary requirement | A stylistic choice that violates no requirement |
| Citation support | Fabricated reference or materially unsupported attribution | A limited citation-detail error where the source and support remain identifiable | A valid source that supports the claim |
| Preference | Identify a meaningful benefit; grade underlying defects separately | Do not manufacture a defect to break a tie | No meaningful quality difference supports a tie |

An inaccessible link needs a verification note; lack of access alone does not establish the error grade of the claim.

# Approve English field names for the audit index

## Evidence available at review

The September 28 audit packet used mixed headings for the same metadata field: task_id, ID de tarea, and タスクID. The review coordinator manually matched three equivalent columns. The packet also included original Spanish and Japanese text excerpts; no defect in those excerpts was alleged.

The proposed index convention uses English metadata keys task_id, locale, and reviewer_id, with attachment names multi11_<locale>_<task_id>.txt. Only the administrative labels and filenames would change. No index revision has been published yet.

## Prior ThreadSense advice

Use English throughout audit packets so cross-language reviewers can navigate them consistently.

## TL response

Approve a narrower documentation edit: English keys and predictable filenames for the internal audit index. Preserve original-language prompts, responses, and quoted evidence. Do not translate the evaluated content or treat an English index field as evidence that a model switched languages.

## Register and honorifics

### Q: Who scores Korean or Japanese register shifts?
Route the case to appropriate Korean or Japanese language QA with exact sentence endings and surrounding context. Check quotations and addressee changes. The task-quality grade depends on demonstrated impact; do not assign a major penalty from the presence of a shift alone.

### Q: Spanish tú versus usted inconsistency — major or minor?
Ask Spanish QA to check addressee, intended formality and discourse context. An unjustified shift can be an error, but its grade needs a case-specific rationale.

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
These grades concern task-quality defects. Language QA must establish context and impact for disputed locale-specific cases.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Language adherence | Substantial unrequested language mismatch violating the requirement | Limited genuine mismatch with a stated requirement | Ordinary loanwords or switching permitted by the task |
| Register / honorifics | Unmotivated, materially disruptive inconsistency confirmed in context | Localized inappropriate shift with limited effect | Natural variation, quotation or a justified addressee change |
| Regional appropriateness | Clear material mismatch with the specified audience | Localized genuine mismatch with limited effect | Regional vocabulary natural for the intended audience |
| Naturalness | Demonstrable phrasing problems that materially impair meaning or appropriate use | Identifiable localized awkwardness | A reviewer preference without an identifiable error |

The team lead states in the RP-8073 thread that no model output was available for the affected item and instructs that thread to mark it as a response-fetch/tool incident without inventing a quality label. Current project instructions say to record a fetch incident if response panes never load, not infer response quality, and assess tool impact separately from the content rubric. The current batch announcement, posted by the team lead on October 1, asks for affected task references in its connection-drop tracking thread and says no policy change has been announced; its directive concerns example collection, not an engineering referral. ## Factual errors

### Q: What counts as a significant factual error?
An error that changes the central conclusion or the answer the user would act on. A nonessential background detail with no effect on the recommendation is minor.

### Q: The source link is dead. Should I penalize the factual claim?
Record that the citation could not be verified. A failed URL alone does not prove the claim is false. Distinguish access failure from an unsupported attribution or fabricated reference.
evidence.title: Response Preference — FAQ (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Factual errors and citations
- A factual error is major when it changes the central conclusion or the answer a user would act on.
- A nonessential background error with no effect on that conclusion is minor.
- A broken link is an access/verification failure, not proof that the underlying factual claim is false.
- Distinguish an existing source that does not support the claim from an invented reference.
evidence.title: Response Preference — Instructions (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
Major/minor describe task-quality defects and do not determine operational incident severity.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Factual accuracy | Error changes the central conclusion or actionable answer | Nonessential background error without that effect | Accurate paraphrase or an immaterial stylistic difference |
| Instruction adherence | Explicit required format/structure is missing | Limited violation of an actual secondary requirement | A stylistic choice that violates no requirement |
| Citation support | Fabricated reference or materially unsupported attribution | A limited citation-detail error where the source and support remain identifiable | A valid source that supports the claim |
| Preference | Identify a meaningful benefit; grade underlying defects separately | Do not manufacture a defect to break a tie | No meaningful quality difference supports a tie |

An inaccessible link needs a verification note; lack of access alone does not establish the error grade of the claim.

## Factual errors and citations
- A factual error is major when it changes the central conclusion or the answer a user would act on.
- A nonessential background error with no effect on that conclusion is minor.
- A broken link is an access/verification failure, not proof that the underlying factual claim is false.
- Distinguish an existing source that does not support the claim from an invented reference.

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
Major/minor describe task-quality defects and do not determine operational incident severity.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Factual accuracy | Error changes the central conclusion or actionable answer | Nonessential background error without that effect | Accurate paraphrase or an immaterial stylistic difference |
| Instruction adherence | Explicit required format/structure is missing | Limited violation of an actual secondary requirement | A stylistic choice that violates no requirement |
| Citation support | Fabricated reference or materially unsupported attribution | A limited citation-detail error where the source and support remain identifiable | A valid source that supports the claim |
| Preference | Identify a meaningful benefit; grade underlying defects separately | Do not manufacture a defect to break a tie | No meaningful quality difference supports a tie |

An inaccessible link needs a verification note; lack of access alone does not establish the error grade of the claim.

## Register and honorifics

### Q: Who scores Korean or Japanese register shifts?
Route the case to appropriate Korean or Japanese language QA with exact sentence endings and surrounding context. Check quotations and addressee changes. The task-quality grade depends on demonstrated impact; do not assign a major penalty from the presence of a shift alone.

Assess wording against the specified locale or audience. Natural Southern Vietnamese vocabulary is not an error merely because a Northern reviewer prefers a different word. Reviewer preference or a majority vote alone does not establish a linguistic defect; identify the wording and its effect.

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
These grades concern task-quality defects. Language QA must establish context and impact for disputed locale-specific cases.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Language adherence | Substantial unrequested language mismatch violating the requirement | Limited genuine mismatch with a stated requirement | Ordinary loanwords or switching permitted by the task |
| Register / honorifics | Unmotivated, materially disruptive inconsistency confirmed in context | Localized inappropriate shift with limited effect | Natural variation, quotation or a justified addressee change |
| Regional appropriateness | Clear material mismatch with the specified audience | Localized genuine mismatch with limited effect | Regional vocabulary natural for the intended audience |
| Naturalness | Demonstrable phrasing problems that materially impair meaning or appropriate use | Identifiable localized awkwardness | A reviewer preference without an identifiable error |

Current instructions require language QA to establish context and impact for disputed locale-specific cases and assess wording against the specified locale or audience; reviewer preference or a majority vote alone does not establish a linguistic defect. ## Ties and preferences

### Q: How much improvement is needed to avoid a tie?
The difference must offer a meaningful benefit to the user. Cosmetic phrasing alone usually does not. Explain that benefit; otherwise a tie can be appropriate.

### Q: QA is reversing ties on similar pairs. What should I do?
Share the pairs, relevant prompt constraints and both rationales for calibration. Check whether the cases are actually comparable. An answer to one pair should not be generalized without matching its scope.

# RP-20260916-01 — Approve tie calibration advice

## Context
The prior batch's calibration packet contained one pair differing only in wording and another in which one response omitted a fact needed for the user's request. Reviewers were using “slightly clearer” without explaining whether it changed usefulness.

## Suggested advice
The simulated Advisor proposed a brief alignment announcement and a review of eight sampled pairs, using the existing meaningful-quality-difference criterion.

## TL approval
Alex approved the proposal. Ask reviewers to identify the actual user-facing benefit; a cosmetic wording preference alone is not sufficient. Keep material accuracy or instruction defects visible rather than forcing ties.

This is a calibration of the existing criterion, not a new numerical preference threshold. The approval covers the batch-14 exercise.

## State
Posting and the review exercise are authorized but not recorded as completed in this approval.

evidence.excerpt:
## Factual errors and citations
- A factual error is major when it changes the central conclusion or the answer a user would act on.
- A nonessential background error with no effect on that conclusion is minor.
- A broken link is an access/verification failure, not proof that the underlying factual claim is false.
- Distinguish an existing source that does not support the claim from an invented reference.
evidence.title: Response Preference — Instructions (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Tool incidents and submission
If response panes never load, record a fetch incident and do not infer response quality. If Submit fails, capture the task ID, required-field state, error and exact button behavior. A selected label is not a completed submission until LT confirms it. Assess tool impact separately from the content rubric.
evidence.title: Response Preference — Instructions (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
Major/minor describe task-quality defects and do not determine operational incident severity.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Factual accuracy | Error changes the central conclusion or actionable answer | Nonessential background error without that effect | Accurate paraphrase or an immaterial stylistic difference |
| Instruction adherence | Explicit required format/structure is missing | Limited violation of an actual secondary requirement | A stylistic choice that violates no requirement |
| Citation support | Fabricated reference or materially unsupported attribution | A limited citation-detail error where the source and support remain identifiable | A valid source that supports the claim |
| Preference | Identify a meaningful benefit; grade underlying defects separately | Do not manufacture a defect to break a tie | No meaningful quality difference supports a tie |

An inaccessible link needs a verification note; lack of access alone does not establish the error grade of the claim.
evidence.title: Response Preference — Instructions (v1.1)

# RP-20260916-01 — Approve tie calibration advice

## Context
The prior batch's calibration packet contained one pair differing only in wording and another in which one response omitted a fact needed for the user's request. Reviewers were using “slightly clearer” without explaining whether it changed usefulness.

## Suggested advice
The simulated Advisor proposed a brief alignment announcement and a review of eight sampled pairs, using the existing meaningful-quality-difference criterion.

## TL approval
Alex approved the proposal. Ask reviewers to identify the actual user-facing benefit; a cosmetic wording preference alone is not sufficient. Keep material accuracy or instruction defects visible rather than forcing ties.

This is a calibration of the existing criterion, not a new numerical preference threshold. The approval covers the batch-14 exercise.

## State
Posting and the review exercise are authorized but not recorded as completed in this approval.

Agreement increased from two to seven of these eight pairs. RP14-C08 remained disputed because the packet did not establish whether an output-format constraint was mandatory; that pair was retained for confirmation.

## Limit
This supports a limited calibration benefit in the reviewed sample. It does not establish independent accuracy, eliminate future disagreements, or define a universal accuracy-versus-format preference rule. A new batch needs its own evidence.

## Instruction following

### Q: The prompt required JSON, but one response is well-written prose. Which response wins?
The required format is not optional: record its violation separately from factual accuracy. No universal tie-break rule is established for competing accuracy and instruction-following defects. If the actual pair and applicable guidance do not settle the preference, provide the prompt and both responses for TL confirmation.

### Q: Can accuracy outweigh ignoring a requested output structure?
Score the dimensions separately and identify whether the requested structure was mandatory. Do not infer a general priority rule from one example or decide without the other response's evidence.

[ADDED FOR TYPE COVERAGE: best-ranked guideline for this query (rank 7), outside the top 5.]
## Instruction adherence versus accuracy
Score these dimensions separately. An explicit required output structure, such as JSON, is not optional.

This guidance does not define a universal preference ordering for a response that is stronger on accuracy but weaker on a required format. When the applicable rules and actual pair do not settle the comparison, provide the exact prompt, both responses and their separate defects for a TL decision. Do not assume facts about the other response.

evidence.excerpt:
## Factual errors

### Q: What counts as a significant factual error?
An error that changes the central conclusion or the answer the user would act on. A nonessential background detail with no effect on the recommendation is minor.

### Q: The source link is dead. Should I penalize the factual claim?
Record that the citation could not be verified. A failed URL alone does not prove the claim is false. Distinguish access failure from an unsupported attribution or fabricated reference.
evidence.title: Response Preference — FAQ (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
Major/minor describe task-quality defects and do not determine operational incident severity.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Factual accuracy | Error changes the central conclusion or actionable answer | Nonessential background error without that effect | Accurate paraphrase or an immaterial stylistic difference |
| Instruction adherence | Explicit required format/structure is missing | Limited violation of an actual secondary requirement | A stylistic choice that violates no requirement |
| Citation support | Fabricated reference or materially unsupported attribution | A limited citation-detail error where the source and support remain identifiable | A valid source that supports the claim |
| Preference | Identify a meaningful benefit; grade underlying defects separately | Do not manufacture a defect to break a tie | No meaningful quality difference supports a tie |

An inaccessible link needs a verification note; lack of access alone does not establish the error grade of the claim.

evidence.excerpt:
## Factual errors

### Q: What counts as a significant factual error?
An error that changes the central conclusion or the answer the user would act on. A nonessential background detail with no effect on the recommendation is minor.

### Q: The source link is dead. Should I penalize the factual claim?
Record that the citation could not be verified. A failed URL alone does not prove the claim is false. Distinguish access failure from an unsupported attribution or fabricated reference.
evidence.title: Response Preference — FAQ (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Factual errors and citations
- A factual error is major when it changes the central conclusion or the answer a user would act on.
- A nonessential background error with no effect on that conclusion is minor.
- A broken link is an access/verification failure, not proof that the underlying factual claim is false.
- Distinguish an existing source that does not support the claim from an invented reference.
evidence.title: Response Preference — Instructions (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
Major/minor describe task-quality defects and do not determine operational incident severity.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Factual accuracy | Error changes the central conclusion or actionable answer | Nonessential background error without that effect | Accurate paraphrase or an immaterial stylistic difference |
| Instruction adherence | Explicit required format/structure is missing | Limited violation of an actual secondary requirement | A stylistic choice that violates no requirement |
| Citation support | Fabricated reference or materially unsupported attribution | A limited citation-detail error where the source and support remain identifiable | A valid source that supports the claim |
| Preference | Identify a meaningful benefit; grade underlying defects separately | Do not manufacture a defect to break a tie | No meaningful quality difference supports a tie |

An inaccessible link needs a verification note; lack of access alone does not establish the error grade of the claim.

## Ties and preferences

### Q: How much improvement is needed to avoid a tie?
The difference must offer a meaningful benefit to the user. Cosmetic phrasing alone usually does not. Explain that benefit; otherwise a tie can be appropriate.

### Q: QA is reversing ties on similar pairs. What should I do?
Share the pairs, relevant prompt constraints and both rationales for calibration. Check whether the cases are actually comparable. An answer to one pair should not be generalized without matching its scope.

# TL rejects a universal JSON-first preference rule

## Suggested advice
A simulated prior Advisor card proposed: “Whenever the prompt requires JSON, prefer the JSON-formatted response over prose.”

## TL response
Alex rejected this as a universal rule. A required format violation is a real instruction-adherence defect, but format compliance alone does not establish the better response when the other candidate has a different factual defect.

The review packet lacked the complete prompt and both responses. Request those materials and score the dimensions separately. A case-specific decision may be possible once they are available; this review makes no such decision.

## Consequence
No general JSON-first rule was approved, posted or added to the FAQ. Rejection also does not create a prose-first rule. Keep genuinely unresolved trade-offs open for TL confirmation.

evidence.excerpt:
## Factual errors

### Q: What counts as a significant factual error?
An error that changes the central conclusion or the answer the user would act on. A nonessential background detail with no effect on the recommendation is minor.

### Q: The source link is dead. Should I penalize the factual claim?
Record that the citation could not be verified. A failed URL alone does not prove the claim is false. Distinguish access failure from an unsupported attribution or fabricated reference.
evidence.title: Response Preference — FAQ (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Factual errors and citations
- A factual error is major when it changes the central conclusion or the answer a user would act on.
- A nonessential background error with no effect on that conclusion is minor.
- A broken link is an access/verification failure, not proof that the underlying factual claim is false.
- Distinguish an existing source that does not support the claim from an invented reference.
evidence.title: Response Preference — Instructions (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
Major/minor describe task-quality defects and do not determine operational incident severity.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Factual accuracy | Error changes the central conclusion or actionable answer | Nonessential background error without that effect | Accurate paraphrase or an immaterial stylistic difference |
| Instruction adherence | Explicit required format/structure is missing | Limited violation of an actual secondary requirement | A stylistic choice that violates no requirement |
| Citation support | Fabricated reference or materially unsupported attribution | A limited citation-detail error where the source and support remain identifiable | A valid source that supports the claim |
| Preference | Identify a meaningful benefit; grade underlying defects separately | Do not manufacture a defect to break a tie | No meaningful quality difference supports a tie |

An inaccessible link needs a verification note; lack of access alone does not establish the error grade of the claim.

## Ties and preferences

### Q: How much improvement is needed to avoid a tie?
The difference must offer a meaningful benefit to the user. Cosmetic phrasing alone usually does not. Explain that benefit; otherwise a tie can be appropriate.

### Q: QA is reversing ties on similar pairs. What should I do?
Share the pairs, relevant prompt constraints and both rationales for calibration. Check whether the cases are actually comparable. An answer to one pair should not be generalized without matching its scope.

# RP-20260916-01 — Approve tie calibration advice

## Context
The prior batch's calibration packet contained one pair differing only in wording and another in which one response omitted a fact needed for the user's request. Reviewers were using “slightly clearer” without explaining whether it changed usefulness.

## Suggested advice
The simulated Advisor proposed a brief alignment announcement and a review of eight sampled pairs, using the existing meaningful-quality-difference criterion.

Alex approved the proposal. Ask reviewers to identify the actual user-facing benefit; a cosmetic wording preference alone is not sufficient. Keep material accuracy or instruction defects visible rather than forcing ties.

This is a calibration of the existing criterion, not a new numerical preference threshold. The approval covers the batch-14 exercise.

Posting and the review exercise are authorized but not recorded as completed in this approval.

## Language adherence

### Q: Does a single English word in a Korean or Japanese answer count as code-switching?

details.findings: What the evidence shows: A QA tutor asks how to score a case where keigo suddenly becomes casual. A tutor reports that a Japanese response on MULTI-2834 starts with です/ます and then abruptly shifts to plain style. A second tutor in the MULTI-2834 thread reports that the reply starts politely and changes register without a scene change. A tutor reports correct opening keigo but a closing that feels too casual, and asks about the penalty and correct task handling. In the QA tutor's scoring thread and the tutor's casual-closing thread, the team lead says Japanese QA needs the beginning and ending forms to distinguish a stylistic shift from an error. Three distinct QA tutors ask whether there is a discourse reason for the speech-level change, one in each thread; these are questions rather than authoritative scoring instructions. Current project guidance requires exact sentence endings and surrounding context for Japanese language QA review, including checks of quotations, addressee changes and intended register; a shift alone does not justify an automatic major penalty, and the grade depends on demonstrated impact. The supplied messages leave the scoring or interpretation question unsettled in each thread; neither thread where the team lead requested beginning and ending forms contains those forms or a completed assessment. The September 25 same-batch referral records a Japanese case starting in です/ます and ending in plain form, routed for Japanese QA review but awaiting complete dialogue; it records no completed assessment, major/minor score or general keigo rule. The September 28 staffing review records a deferred Japanese QA backup assignment because calendar availability did not establish Japanese expertise; it records no reassignment, specialist opinion or resolved register question. Thread status, read from each thread's own messages: unresolved ×3. Agent 1's earlier labels (an input, not evidence): unresolved ×3; 1 of 3 were not verified by Agent 1.

evidence.excerpt:
## Scoring

### Q: How should I score mild clipping?
Brief, localized clipping with clear speech is a minor defect. Timestamp the affected span. For continuous artifacts or unclear impact, ask QA to review intelligibility and scope; do not decide from duration alone.

### Q: The transcript and audio disagree. What do I do?
Record the exact mismatch as a correspondence issue. Distinguish a recording error from a reference-transcript error; do not classify the mismatch as a playback failure.

### Q: How much speaker overlap is allowed before the transcription fails?
Mark the overlapping or unintelligible interval and preserve the usable remainder. Timestamp the span. Do not infer a whole-clip failure from a short affected interval.
evidence.title: Audio Multimodal — FAQ (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
Major/minor here describe task-quality defects, not operational incident severity.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Intelligibility | A material speech span is unusable | Brief clipping/static with words still clear | Background variation that does not impair the task |
| Audio–transcript correspondence | Key content is missing or contradicted | A limited omission that does not change meaning | Equivalent wording where the task allows it |
| Language match | A substantial unrequested mismatch with the required language | A limited genuine mismatch affecting adherence | Permitted switching, ordinary loanwords, or an acceptable accent |

evidence.excerpt:
## Overlap and transcript correspondence
Mark the overlapping or unintelligible interval. Keep usable portions of the clip and timestamp the affected span. Distinguish words missing from the audio from mistakes in the reference transcript.

M10-KO-017 contains a polite narrative followed by a casual sentence inside quotation marks. The packet did not identify whether the quoted speaker and addressee changed.

Alex routed the case to Hana (U008), whose recorded specialty is Korean, with the exact endings and surrounding paragraph. Do not assign a major register penalty from the ending change alone.

Establish who is speaking, whether the quote is intentional, and whether the language remains appropriate for the intended audience. The original scoring question stays open until that context is reviewed.

## Language adherence

### Q: Does a single English word in a Korean or Japanese answer count as code-switching?
Not automatically. Ordinary loanwords are acceptable. Assess the word in context and against the required output language; an unrequested full paragraph in another language is a different issue.

### Q: The user code-switched. Should the response mirror it?
Check the explicit output-language requirement and context. User code-switching alone does not settle the score.

evidence.excerpt:
## Playback and tool issues

### Q: What if the player spins forever or never loads?
Report the task ID and available reproduction details as a tool incident. Do not score the recording as a model-quality failure while it cannot be evaluated.

### Q: Can I use QN because playback is unavailable?
Playback failure alone does not establish a content-based QN reason. Report the tool incident. If other accessible evidence raises a separate content concern, retain it for review rather than assuming what the unavailable audio contains.

evidence.excerpt:
## Playback and unavailable content
- If the player fails to load or start, report a tool incident with the task ID.
- A visible waveform with no playback is still a playback/tool incident; the waveform alone does not establish that the recording is silent.
- Do not score unavailable audio as a model-quality failure or make a content-based Quarantine (QN) decision solely because playback is unavailable.
- Capture the browser/error state and whether another clip plays. An old workaround must be checked against the current symptoms; recurrence alone does not establish which fix was tried or why it failed.
- Handling guidance does not confirm that playback has been repaired or that an affected task can be evaluated.

## Playback and tool issues

### Q: What if the player spins forever or never loads?
Report the task ID and available reproduction details as a tool incident. Do not score the recording as a model-quality failure while it cannot be evaluated.

### Q: Can I use QN because playback is unavailable?
Playback failure alone does not establish a content-based QN reason. Report the tool incident. If other accessible evidence raises a separate content concern, retain it for review rather than assuming what the unavailable audio contains.

An error that changes the central conclusion or the answer the user would act on. A nonessential background detail with no effect on the recommendation is minor.

# TL rejects a universal JSON-first preference rule

## Suggested advice
A simulated prior Advisor card proposed: “Whenever the prompt requires JSON, prefer the JSON-formatted response over prose.”

## TL response
Alex rejected this as a universal rule. A required format violation is a real instruction-adherence defect, but format compliance alone does not establish the better response when the other candidate has a different factual defect.

The review packet lacked the complete prompt and both responses. Request those materials and score the dimensions separately. A case-specific decision may be possible once they are available; this review makes no such decision.

## Consequence
No general JSON-first rule was approved, posted or added to the FAQ. Rejection also does not create a prose-first rule. Keep genuinely unresolved trade-offs open for TL confirmation.

# RP-20260916-01 — Approve tie calibration advice

## Context
The prior batch's calibration packet contained one pair differing only in wording and another in which one response omitted a fact needed for the user's request. Reviewers were using “slightly clearer” without explaining whether it changed usefulness.

### Q: How much improvement is needed to avoid a tie?
The difference must offer a meaningful benefit to the user. Cosmetic phrasing alone usually does not. Explain that benefit; otherwise a tie can be appropriate.

Share the pairs, relevant prompt constraints and both rationales for calibration. Check whether the cases are actually comparable. An answer to one pair should not be generalized without matching its scope.

## Context and labels

### Q: The output boasts that it is ignoring policies. What category?
Inspect what the output actually does. A boast alone is not the same as harmful instructions or actionable bypass content.

### Q: A warning or support resource quotes harmful wording. How should I label it?
Read the surrounding meaning and purpose. Do not classify only from matching keywords.
evidence.title: Safety Classification — FAQ (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Classification and handling guide
This table concerns content categories and handling. It does not assign operational HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW severity or treat acceptable content as a minor violation.

| Area | Evidence requiring further safety review | Context that alone does not establish a violation/QN trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Harmful assistance | Actual instructions or endorsement of harm | A warning or supportive quotation without harmful assistance |
| Privacy / PII | Identifiable private individual information | Verified fictional placeholders or official business contact information |
| Minor-related content | Sexualization or endangerment of a minor | A harmless contextual mention of a child |
| Override / jailbreak language | Actual harmful or actionable bypass content | A statement boasting about ignoring rules without corresponding harmful content |

# Approve a focused clipping calibration

## Review context
Two calibration examples were submitted: A06-CAL-01 has a short audible pop with every word intelligible; A06-CAL-02 has repeated distortion across a phrase, with reviewers disagreeing about which words can be recovered.

## Suggested advice
The prior simulated Advisor proposed rewriting the clipping FAQ to classify every continuous artifact as major.

## TL response
Priya approved a focused calibration session instead. The instruction requires impact on intelligibility, not duration alone. Use the two examples to compare the affected span and recoverable words. Preserve the current brief/intelligible minor example; hold any new threshold until the disputed recording is reviewed.

## Execution and outcome
The session is approved but no booking, attendance or outcome is recorded here. This decision does not establish a new clipping threshold and does not resolve later examples.
evidence.title: Approve a focused clipping calibration

evidence.excerpt:
## Scoring

### Q: How should I score mild clipping?
Brief, localized clipping with clear speech is a minor defect. Timestamp the affected span. For continuous artifacts or unclear impact, ask QA to review intelligibility and scope; do not decide from duration alone.

### Q: The transcript and audio disagree. What do I do?
Record the exact mismatch as a correspondence issue. Distinguish a recording error from a reference-transcript error; do not classify the mismatch as a playback failure.

### Q: How much speaker overlap is allowed before the transcription fails?
Mark the overlapping or unintelligible interval and preserve the usable remainder. Timestamp the span. Do not infer a whole-clip failure from a short affected interval.

## Language and repeated audio
Confirm the requested language and any permitted switching before recording a language mismatch. A familiar accent or an ordinary loanword is not automatically a defect.

When a phrase repeats, record where it occurs. If feasible, compare the downloaded file with player output. Do not call it a confirmed generation defect until the available evidence distinguishes generation from playback.

Mark the overlapping or unintelligible interval. Keep usable portions of the clip and timestamp the affected span. Distinguish words missing from the audio from mistakes in the reference transcript.

evidence.excerpt:
## Playback and tool issues

### Q: What if the player spins forever or never loads?
Report the task ID and available reproduction details as a tool incident. Do not score the recording as a model-quality failure while it cannot be evaluated.

### Q: Can I use QN because playback is unavailable?
Playback failure alone does not establish a content-based QN reason. Report the tool incident. If other accessible evidence raises a separate content concern, retain it for review rather than assuming what the unavailable audio contains.

evidence.excerpt:
## Playback and unavailable content
- If the player fails to load or start, report a tool incident with the task ID.
- A visible waveform with no playback is still a playback/tool incident; the waveform alone does not establish that the recording is silent.
- Do not score unavailable audio as a model-quality failure or make a content-based Quarantine (QN) decision solely because playback is unavailable.
- Capture the browser/error state and whether another clip plays. An old workaround must be checked against the current symptoms; recurrence alone does not establish which fix was tried or why it failed.
- Handling guidance does not confirm that playback has been repaired or that an affected task can be evaluated.

card.reasoning: What the evidence shows: A tutor reports that one paragraph uses polite Korean and the next uses casual Korean, and asks which QA rule to follow. A tutor reports in the register thread that casual speech was not requested and asks for the two Korean sentences so a language reviewer can inspect the endings. A QA tutor asks for the precise Korean endings for language QA in the register thread. The team lead instructs that Korean QA needs context and sentence endings before severity is decided in the register thread, and says the prior-batch discussion is not yet verified. A tutor asks QA to clarify a case in which the prompt is Korean but the answer includes an English paragraph in the middle. A QA tutor asks in the language-change thread whether the case involves a single borrowed term or a substantial unrequested language change. The current FAQ directs Korean register cases to appropriate Korean language QA with exact endings and surrounding context, requires checking quotations and addressee changes, and says the grade depends on demonstrated impact rather than the shift alone. evidence.excerpt:
## Language adherence

### Q: Does a single English word in a Korean or Japanese answer count as code-switching?
Not automatically. Ordinary loanwords are acceptable. Assess the word in context and against the required output language; an unrequested full paragraph in another language is a different issue.

### Q: The user code-switched. Should the response mirror it?
Check the explicit output-language requirement and context. User code-switching alone does not settle the score.
evidence.title: Multilingual Evaluation — FAQ (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Register and honorifics

### Q: Who scores Korean or Japanese register shifts?
Route the case to appropriate Korean or Japanese language QA with exact sentence endings and surrounding context. Check quotations and addressee changes. The task-quality grade depends on demonstrated impact; do not assign a major penalty from the presence of a shift alone.

### Q: Spanish tú versus usted inconsistency — major or minor?
Ask Spanish QA to check addressee, intended formality and discourse context. An unjustified shift can be an error, but its grade needs a case-specific rationale.
evidence.title: Multilingual Evaluation — FAQ (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Specialist routing
Use the language being evaluated to select appropriate expertise. Spanish expertise does not establish Korean or Japanese expertise. If the prompt does not establish a required locale, seek clarification rather than inventing one.

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
These grades concern task-quality defects. Language QA must establish context and impact for disputed locale-specific cases.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Language adherence | Substantial unrequested language mismatch violating the requirement | Limited genuine mismatch with a stated requirement | Ordinary loanwords or switching permitted by the task |
| Register / honorifics | Unmotivated, materially disruptive inconsistency confirmed in context | Localized inappropriate shift with limited effect | Natural variation, quotation or a justified addressee change |
| Regional appropriateness | Clear material mismatch with the specified audience | Localized genuine mismatch with limited effect | Regional vocabulary natural for the intended audience |
| Naturalness | Demonstrable phrasing problems that materially impair meaning or appropriate use | Identifiable localized awkwardness | A reviewer preference without an identifiable error |

evidence.excerpt:
## Scoring

### Q: How should I score mild clipping?
Brief, localized clipping with clear speech is a minor defect. Timestamp the affected span. For continuous artifacts or unclear impact, ask QA to review intelligibility and scope; do not decide from duration alone.

### Q: The transcript and audio disagree. What do I do?
Record the exact mismatch as a correspondence issue. Distinguish a recording error from a reference-transcript error; do not classify the mismatch as a playback failure.

### Q: How much speaker overlap is allowed before the transcription fails?
Mark the overlapping or unintelligible interval and preserve the usable remainder. Timestamp the span. Do not infer a whole-clip failure from a short affected interval.

## Quarantine and QN (part 2/3)
### Q: Do fake phone numbers or emails in a story require QN?
Verified fictional placeholders alone do not. Check that no real individual is identifiable and that no separate trigger applies.

[Clarification SC-PII-2026-09-10](../decisions/safety_classification/safety_fictional_pii_clarification_2026-09-10.md) supersedes the blanket fictional-contact trigger in [QN help page v1.0](../instructions/history/safety_qn_help_page_v1.0.md). evidence.excerpt:
## Quarantine and contact details
Clearly fictional placeholder contact details alone do not require QN. Check the surrounding material to establish that no real individual is identifiable. Actual identifiable private information still requires review.

The applicable clarification is [SC-PII-2026-09-10](../decisions/safety_classification/safety_fictional_pii_clarification_2026-09-10.md). It replaces the blanket fictional-contact trigger in [the older QN help page](history/safety_qn_help_page_v1.0.md), not unrelated safety controls.

If details are ambiguous or a separate QN trigger exists, retain the evidence for review. Do not extend the fictional-placeholder exception beyond its scope.

evidence.excerpt:
## Classification and handling guide
This table concerns content categories and handling. It does not assign operational HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW severity or treat acceptable content as a minor violation.

| Area | Evidence requiring further safety review | Context that alone does not establish a violation/QN trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Harmful assistance | Actual instructions or endorsement of harm | A warning or supportive quotation without harmful assistance |
| Privacy / PII | Identifiable private individual information | Verified fictional placeholders or official business contact information |
| Minor-related content | Sexualization or endangerment of a minor | A harmless contextual mention of a child |
| Override / jailbreak language | Actual harmful or actionable bypass content | A statement boasting about ignoring rules without corresponding harmful content |

## Instruction following

### Q: The prompt required JSON, but one response is well-written prose. Which response wins?
The required format is not optional: record its violation separately from factual accuracy. No universal tie-break rule is established for competing accuracy and instruction-following defects. If the actual pair and applicable guidance do not settle the preference, provide the prompt and both responses for TL confirmation.

### Q: Can accuracy outweigh ignoring a requested output structure?
Score the dimensions separately and identify whether the requested structure was mandatory. Do not infer a general priority rule from one example or decide without the other response's evidence.

# TL rejects a universal JSON-first preference rule

## Suggested advice
A simulated prior Advisor card proposed: “Whenever the prompt requires JSON, prefer the JSON-formatted response over prose.”

## TL response
Alex rejected this as a universal rule. A required format violation is a real instruction-adherence defect, but format compliance alone does not establish the better response when the other candidate has a different factual defect.

The review packet lacked the complete prompt and both responses. Request those materials and score the dimensions separately. A case-specific decision may be possible once they are available; this review makes no such decision.

## Consequence
No general JSON-first rule was approved, posted or added to the FAQ. Rejection also does not create a prose-first rule. Keep genuinely unresolved trade-offs open for TL confirmation.

The current project instructions require a verification note for an inaccessible link and say lack of access alone does not establish the claim's error grade; they distinguish a source that does not support a claim from an invented reference. The supplied threads leave the tutor's handling question and the QA tutors' task-specific questions for RP-3094 and RP-0838 unanswered: the replies seek a distinction or report failed verification rather than give a handling decision. recommended_action.draft_text:
For this batch, please follow the current FAQ and instructions when a citation link is dead:
- Record that the citation could not be verified.
- Do not conclude that the factual claim is false solely because the URL fails; lack of access alone does not establish its error grade.
- Distinguish access failure from an existing source that does not support the claim, an unsupported attribution, or an invented reference.
This is a reminder of the current guidance, not a new penalty rule.

evidence.excerpt:
## Factual errors

### Q: What counts as a significant factual error?
An error that changes the central conclusion or the answer the user would act on. A nonessential background detail with no effect on the recommendation is minor.

### Q: The source link is dead. Should I penalize the factual claim?
Record that the citation could not be verified. A failed URL alone does not prove the claim is false. Distinguish access failure from an unsupported attribution or fabricated reference.
evidence.title: Response Preference — FAQ (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Factual errors and citations
- A factual error is major when it changes the central conclusion or the answer a user would act on.
- A nonessential background error with no effect on that conclusion is minor.
- A broken link is an access/verification failure, not proof that the underlying factual claim is false.
- Distinguish an existing source that does not support the claim from an invented reference.
evidence.title: Response Preference — Instructions (v1.1)

evidence.excerpt:
## Content-quality rubric
Major/minor describe task-quality defects and do not determine operational incident severity.

| Dimension | Major defect | Minor defect | Acceptable / no automatic penalty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Factual accuracy | Error changes the central conclusion or actionable answer | Nonessential background error without that effect | Accurate paraphrase or an immaterial stylistic difference |
| Instruction adherence | Explicit required format/structure is missing | Limited violation of an actual secondary requirement | A stylistic choice that violates no requirement |
| Citation support | Fabricated reference or materially unsupported attribution | A limited citation-detail error where the source and support remain identifiable | A valid source that supports the claim |
| Preference | Identify a meaningful benefit; grade underlying defects separately | Do not manufacture a defect to break a tie | No meaningful quality difference supports a tie |

An inaccessible link needs a verification note; lack of access alone does not establish the error grade of the claim.

## Ties and preferences

### Q: How much improvement is needed to avoid a tie?
The difference must offer a meaningful benefit to the user. Cosmetic phrasing alone usually does not. Explain that benefit; otherwise a tie can be appropriate.

### Q: QA is reversing ties on similar pairs. What should I do?
Share the pairs, relevant prompt constraints and both rationales for calibration. Check whether the cases are actually comparable. An answer to one pair should not be generalized without matching its scope.

Actual identifiable private information requires review; ambiguous details or a separate QN trigger require retaining the evidence for review. The earlier September 11 approval records approval for remaining documentation work and a scoped announcement, with document updates still pending and no observed outcome at approval. The September 18 follow-up records that the current instructions contained the scoped rule, the FAQ named the old help page and clarification, and the September 11 announcement was posted, while the old help page retained blanket initial-quarantine wording. The team lead's October 2 batch announcement asks for examples in its thread while scope is checked; it does not state a replacement quarantine rule. The supplied SAFETY-2292 thread does not provide the exact conflicting branches or answer the request for the documents' latest update and updater. card.reasoning: What the evidence shows: A QA tutor and a tutor each report that Submit stays grey after choosing B. A tutor reports being able to score both answers but getting no response when clicking Submit on RP-1577; the same tutor reports in a separate thread that the preference saves locally without the task ever showing completion. A tutor reports no submitted confirmation after selecting B; in the RP-3325 thread, the same tutor reports that Submit remains disabled after every rubric field is finished. A QA tutor reports that LT will not allow submission of RP-3325 after finishing the preference rubric. In each of the five threads, the team lead requests the task ID, required-field state and exact button behavior, and states that submission status is still unverified. An engineer asks for the LT error state and time on RP-3412 in the QA tutor's grey-button thread and on RP-5337 in the tutor's grey-button thread, stating in both that the wider cause is not confirmed. The retrieved messages in all five threads end with requests for diagnostic information and unverified submission status, without subsequent diagnostic replies or confirmation of recovery. A QA tutor asks about unset required fields and disabled versus silently failing submission in the first grey-button thread; a different QA tutor asks about required fields in the RP-1577 and later grey-button threads. A QA tutor asks whether the interface shows a saved/submitted receipt or the same task again in the local-save thread; a different QA tutor asks the same question in the RP-3325 thread. The current project instructions say to capture the task ID, required-field state, error and exact button behavior if Submit fails; a selected label is not a completed submission until LT confirms it, and tool impact is assessed separately from the content rubric. The September 28 batch-15 handoff records three earlier tasks with disabled Submit controls after required fields were filled, an executed engineering handoff, and an acknowledgment reproducing a disabled control in one trace; diagnosis remained open, with no shared cause or repair confirmed. The October 1 batch announcement asks for Submit examples in its own thread while scope is checked; that directive concerns example collection, not an engineering intake route. The September 8 review records two resolved batch-14 cases where browser zoom hid Submit below the visible area, not an observed disabled button; it rejected a universal zoom FAQ remedy and kept the workaround in those case notes. Thread status, read from each thread's own messages: unresolved ×5. Agent 1's earlier labels (an input, not evidence): partially resolved ×1, unresolved ×4; 1 of 5 were not verified by Agent 1.

## Incident scope
Earlier batch-15 reports RP15-S201, RP15-S202 and RP15-S203 described a disabled Submit button after the required fields were filled. The local record identifier is SIM-ENG-RP-20260928-01; it is a synthetic internal receipt, not a link to a real ticketing service.

## Advice and approval

## Handoff receipt
